story.logline: You owe on your card and pay the minimum each month; nearly all of it goes on interest, so how long until you are clear, and what changes it?

question: Should I keep paying the minimum on my credit card, or pay a fixed amount each month?

source.title: Paying only the minimum on a credit card
source.publisher: Test fixture written for this repo; the numbers are illustrative
quotes: Credit cards make it easy to pay only the minimum each month, often 2% of the balance or $25, whichever is more.
A typical card charges about 22% a year, which works out to just under 2% a month on whatever you still owe.
Paying the minimum, it would take over 20 years to clear, and you would pay far more in interest than you originally borrowed.
Paying a fixed $200 a month instead clears the same balance in about two and a half years, with roughly $1,400 in interest.
Each month the interest is added to your balance.

explain.caption: You owe money on your card. When will you clear it?
You pay the minimum, trusting it will clear the card in time.
Each month, the card company adds interest to what you owe.
But nearly all of the minimum goes on interest.
So years pass. The debt stays. The interest you pay piles up.
New things you buy grow the debt faster than payments cut it.
A fixed amount doesn't shrink with the debt, so it clears sooner.
Now make it yours. Your numbers decide the rest.

simulate.prompt: Try your own balance, rate and payment.

tradeoffs: Paying the minimum leaves more cash free each month, but the debt lasts far longer and the interest keeps adding up.
A fixed amount clears the card sooner and costs less interest, but it takes the same sum from your budget every month, even in a tight one.
Moving the balance to a card with a lower rate, or a 0% offer, can cut the interest, but there may be a transfer fee and a higher rate after the offer ends.
Stopping new spending on the card helps the debt fall, but you need another way to pay for things.
leftOut: The article says $200 a month clears $5,000 in about two and a half years with roughly $1,400 in interest. At 22% with interest added monthly, those payments take about 2.8 years and cost nearer $1,750, so this page does not use the $1,400 figure.
Interest is added once a month here; many cards work it out daily, so real figures differ a little.
Minimum payment rules differ between cards. Here it is 2% of what you owe or $25, whichever is more, as in the article. Check how yours is worked out.
Fees (late, annual, balance transfer) are not included, and the rate is held fixed; real rates can change, and a 0% offer ends after a set time.
Missed or late payments, and their effect on your credit record, are not modelled.
The clock stops at 20 years, so a card that takes longer shows as not cleared within 20 years.
